analysis.one_liner: Phases out "forever chemicals" (PFAS) from products and manufacturing and bans their release into the environment.
analysis.headline: The bill to phase out PFAS never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in five House committees until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set a national policy of eliminating "forever chemicals" — per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), which persist in the body and environment and are linked to serious health harms. It would ban PFAS in carpets, cosmetics, food packaging, furniture, apparel, and other consumer goods within one to five years, require manufacturers and users to phase out all nonessential PFAS uses within ten years, and after ten years make it illegal to release detectable amounts of PFAS into the environment. It would also make federal agencies follow the same PFAS rules as everyone else, create a citizen-suit right to enforce the law, and make it harder for PFAS makers to escape cleanup-liability lawsuits through bankruptcy [S2]. It was introduced by Rep. Betty McCollum with one cosponsor, referred to five House committees, sent to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended [S1] [S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people — especially residents of communities with PFAS-contaminated drinking water, military families near bases where firefighting foam was used, and consumers who would no longer be exposed to PFAS through carpets, food packaging, cosmetics, and clothing. Public water systems, which the bill explicitly excludes from the definition of a regulated "manufacturer," would avoid compliance burdens while benefiting from reduced contamination [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Requires manufacturers to phase out all nonessential PFAS uses within 10 years, with earlier bans on PFAS in carpets, food packaging, juvenile products, cosmetics, and apparel within 1-5 years [S2].

Makes it unlawful after 10 years to release any detectable quantity of PFAS into the environment, with EPA monitoring, inspections, civil penalties, and criminal penalties for reckless violations [S2].
Gives citizens the right to sue PFAS violators and the EPA if it fails to act, and waives federal immunity so government agencies must follow the same PFAS laws as private parties [S2].
Adds protections in bankruptcy for claims arising from PFAS exposure and preserves state-law damage suits, making it harder for chemical makers to limit or escape liability for contamination [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers (such as PFAS producers) and the many product makers that rely on PFAS for water- and stain-resistance, who would face phaseout costs, annual reporting fees, monitoring requirements, penalties, and expanded litigation exposure. Some compliance costs could be passed through to consumers in the prices of affected goods [S2].

drawbacks.text: A full phaseout of nonessential PFAS plus a ban on all detectable releases within 10 years is an aggressive mandate; some critical uses (semiconductors, medical devices, certain safety equipment) depend on PFAS, and the bill's essential-use process only allows designations after a National Academies review completed no later than 3 years after enactment [S2].

Compliance and reporting costs fall on manufacturers and users, from large chemical firms to small businesses using PFAS-containing products, and could be passed to consumers through higher prices for goods like rain gear and furniture [S2].

The expanded liability provisions — preserved state-law damages suits and bankruptcy protections for PFAS claims — increase litigation exposure for any company that manufactured or used PFAS, beyond the direct regulatory phaseout [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health and contamination-reduction benefits would accrue broadly to the public, while the costs fall on a specific set of manufacturers and, partly through prices, on consumers of PFAS-containing goods. The bill's short timelines for some product bans and its reliance on a still-unfinished scientific review of which uses are "essential" are real design risks, but the core phaseout approach with exemptions for essential uses is a serious, structured attempt at the problem.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to five House committees and sent to an Environment subcommittee, and no committee ever acted on it or scheduled it for a floor vote before the Congress ended [S4].

narrative.text: Rep. Betty McCollum introduced the Forever Chemical Regulation and Accountability Act of 2024 on April 18, 2024, with Rep. Chellie Pingree as the bill's sole cosponsor [S1] [S3].

The bill was referred to five committees — Energy and Commerce, Oversight, Science, Space and Technology, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Armed Services — and on April 26, 2024, to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Environment, Manufacturing, and Critical Materials [S4].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever occurred; the bill died at the end of the 118th Congress in January 2025 [S1] [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PFAS manufacturers and consumer-product makers that use PFAS are better off: they avoided the phaseout deadlines, reporting fees, monitoring requirements, and expanded litigation exposure the bill would have imposed [S2].

for.name: Rep. Betty McCollum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which would phase out nonessential PFAS uses and ban PFAS releases [S1] [S2].

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 18, 2024, and sent it to its Environment subcommittee but never held a hearing or markup [S4].

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote during the remainder of the 118th Congress [S4].

against.name: PFAS manufacturers and PFAS-using product industries
against.what_they_did: Have broadly opposed comprehensive PFAS bans and expanded PFAS liability in federal legislative debates throughout this period.

sides.party_line_note: Only two members — both Democrats — ever supported the bill on the record, and no vote was ever taken, so no partisan split on the merits exists in the record [S3] [S4].

industries.note: The bill would force a 10-year phaseout of nonessential PFAS production, impose annual reporting fees and monitoring, ban detectable environmental releases, and preserve state-law damage suits with bankruptcy protections that make it harder to escape cleanup liability [S2]. These companies' revenue depends on continued PFAS production, which is what the bill eliminates.

industries.industry: Consumer goods makers (carpets, cosmetics, apparel, furniture, food packaging)
industries.note: The bill would ban sale of PFAS-containing goods in these categories within one to five years, forcing reformulation [S2]. The same bans are what deliver the public-health benefit to consumers.

industries.industry: Public water systems and waste treatment facilities
industries.note: The bill explicitly excludes water systems and treatment works from the regulated 'manufacturer' and 'user' definitions, so they bear no compliance burden while benefiting from reduced PFAS contamination [S2].
